idiom_name: std::jthread fan-out + std::stop_token (destructor joins at scope exit)
implementation_notes: C++20 std::jthread is the language-level scope: its destructor requests stop and joins, so declaring the children as local jthreads (or a std::vector<std::jthread>) makes the enclosing block the join point and no detached thread can outlive it. Cancellation is cooperative through std::stop_token: give the children one shared stop_source's token so a failure or an external cancel can request_stop() across the whole group. For fixed subtrees std::async futures (C++11) or C++26 std::execution when_all are the alternatives; without C++20 the classic hand-written thread vector plus join loop remains.
pitfalls: A child that never inspects its stop_token turns scope exit into an unbounded wait; blocking calls must be made interruptible or bounded.
Each jthread owns a private stop_source, so parent-to-children cancellation needs one shared stop_source whose token is captured by every child.
An exception escaping a jthread's function calls std::terminate - collect failures in shared state or promises instead of throwing across the thread boundary.

variants.name: std::async futures (C++11 classic)
variants.implementation_notes: The pre-C++20 realization: launch each child with std::async(std::launch::async, ...); the returned std::future owns the child, and a waiting get() - or the destruction of the last future reference - joins it before the scope ends. There is no automatic sibling cancellation, so add a shared std::atomic<bool> stop flag that children poll, or bound each child so the join cannot stall. Choose when the toolchain predates C++20; prefer jthread where it is available.
pitfalls: Calling std::async without an explicit launch::async policy may defer execution to get(), silently serializing the 'concurrent' subtasks.
Dropping a future whose task has not finished blocks in the destructor at an arbitrary point; keep every future alive until the scope's join loop.
Exceptions surface only at get(), so an unjoined future hides both its result and its failure.

variants.name: C++26 std::execution when_all + asynchronous scopes (senders)
variants.implementation_notes: The sender/receiver model turns the scope into a value: when_all joins a fixed group of senders into one sender that can only complete after every child has stopped, and std::execution's asynchronous scopes (scope_token/counting_scope) tie dynamically spawned work to a scope so it cannot be torn down while registered operations exist. Cancellation travels as set_stopped together with the stop tokens in each sender's environment. Choose this when the codebase is already sender-based; otherwise the jthread form is simpler.
pitfalls: Senders are lazy: nothing runs until start/sync_wait, so a forgotten sender is silent omitted work rather than a compiler error.
when_all is only as cancellable as its children - stop tokens must be plumbed through the sender environment for set_stopped to reach the siblings.
Dynamic (unbounded) child sets need a counting scope; when_all only joins the senders named statically.
